I'd have him compare the two on how he'll feel after a year, not on the paycheque alone. Ten percent more pay is real, but a 10 minute bike ride instead of 45 minutes on the subway is roughly an hour and 10 minutes a day back, plus less stress and no transit fare. Other things to ask him about: the caseload and hours, mentorship and growth, and whether the pay gap closes after a first raise or review. If the work and the people are about equal, I'd lean toward the shorter commute.

Short version: an EFT is a bank-to-bank electronic transfer that moves in batches over the domestic clearing system, so it is cheap and usually takes one to a few business days, and it can be returned if something goes wrong. A wire is a one-off, real-time transfer, usually same day, with higher fees, and it is generally final once sent. For merchant payouts that matters: EFT is the normal low-cost rail, and a wire is what you would use when speed or a large amount justifies the fee. The two get mixed up in decks, but they are different rails with different cost, speed and reversibility.
Action: Draft a two-line definition you can drop into the deck or send to sales, and I'd check the exact settlement timings against our own payout docs before it goes out.

Yes, I can take the data side. One thing worth building in: bank-side failures are retried automatically with no merchant action needed, so I'd split first-attempt failures from payouts that stayed failed after retry, otherwise the numbers will overstate the problem.
Action: Pull failed payouts for the last 30 days grouped by receiving bank, with failure reason and retried-vs-final status, from the payouts data in Looker or the warehouse. If I can't find the right source, I'd ask Aisha before guessing. I'll have a summary ready for Wednesday's roadmap prep.

Yes, it used to be in January. The game is played on a Sunday because that is the NFL's main day, and it drifted into February as the season got longer, with more regular-season games and an expanded playoff, so the final landed a week or two later. I believe the last January game was in the early 2000s, but I'd double check the exact year.
Action: None, unless you want me to look up the exact year it first moved.

Your lesson with Carlos is Thursday at 19:30, and the DELE B2 is on Sat 21 Nov, so I'd focus on two things: the subjunctive, which you're working on with him, and the noun-gender exceptions you often miss (el problema, el mapa, el tema, la mano). I'd also check Carlos's emailed homework first so you're ready for Thursday.
Action: Look at your calendar and block two or three short study sessions before Thursday's class, tell you which slots I picked, and put together a short subjunctive and noun-gender practice set.

I don't know yet, and I don't want to guess about outdoor ice. Rinks depend on the temperature, so it's worth checking both the city's rink status and Saturday afternoon's forecast.

A few ideas for Diego's partner: join several waitlists at once, ask each centre if they take infants and what their real wait is, and look at licensed home daycare agencies, which often move faster. A nanny share is another option. Ask about the $10/day program when you call.

Yes, a one-page drill sheet covering your three weak spots: ser vs estar (emotions and locations), por vs para, and the subjunctive after cuando for future events. Your example is right to flag: 'cuando llego a casa te llamo' should be 'cuando llegue a casa te llamo'.
Action: Build the drill sheet with about eight fill-in-the-blank items per section, an answer key at the end, and save it where you keep your Spanish homework, ready for your next lesson.

A heat warning means two or more days of very high heat are forecast; an extended heat warning means the hot spell is expected to last longer, roughly three or more days. The thresholds are roughly daytime highs near 31 and overnight lows near 20, or a humidex of 40 or more. The precautions are the same, just plan for a longer stretch of hot nights.
Action: None.

TFSA: you put in after-tax money, it grows tax-free, and you can withdraw anytime with no tax. RRSP: contributions are tax-deductible now, but you pay tax when you withdraw, so it helps most if your income now is higher than it will be in retirement.
